# On Triangulations Generated by the Largest-Angle $n$-Section Algorithm

**arXiv ID**: 2607.25457v1
**Authors**: Jérôme Michaud, Sergey Korotov
**Published**: 2026-07-28
**Categories**: cs.CG, math.NA
**Comments**: 7 pages, 1 figure
**HTML URL**: https://arxiv.org/html/2607.25457v1

## Abstract

We define a mesh refinement algorithm based on the rule of dividing the largest angles of triangular elements of planar partitions in focus into $n$ equal parts, and analyse the (geometric) properties of triangulations generated by this technique. This largest-angle $n$-section rule is compared with the classical longest-edge $n$-section rule, where it is the longest edges which are split into $n$ equal parts. The longest-edge bisection and trisection are known to produce nondegenerate triangulations (possibly with hanging nodes), but the longest-edge $n$-sections with $n\geq 4$ always produce (infinite) sequences of triangles with minimum angles tending to zero (moreover, their relevant maximum angles tend to $π$), thus breaking the minimum and maximum angle conditions. We show that this degeneration effect is not a consequence of $n$-section itself. For every $n\geq 2$, the largest-angle $n$-sections produce partitions satisfying the minimum angle condition (and, therefore, the maximum angle condition). More precisely, if the initial triangle has its smallest angle $γ_0>0$, then all descendant triangles have angles bounded below by $m_n=\min\left\{γ_0,\fracπ{3n}\right\},$ and, correspondingly, bounded above by $π-2m_n<π$. We also show that the recursive largest-angle $n$-section algorithm always produces a family of triangular partitions, i.e. the maximum diameter of level-$k$ descendants tends to zero as $k \to \infty$.

## On Triangulations Generated by the Largest-Anglenn-Section AlgorithmJérôme Michaud and Sergey Korotov

## Abstract

We define a mesh refinement algorithm based on the rule of dividing the largest angles of triangular elements of planar partitions in focus intonnequal parts, and analyse the (geometric) properties of triangulations generated by this technique. This largest-anglenn-section rule is compared with the classical longest-edgenn-section rule, where it is the longest edges which are split intonnequal parts. The longest-edge bisection and trisection are known to produce nondegenerate triangulations (possibly with hanging nodes), but the longest-edgenn-sections withn≥4n\geq 4always produce (infinite) sequences of triangles with minimum angles tending to zero (moreover, their relevant maximum angles tend toπ\pi), thus breaking the minimum and maximum angle conditions. We show that this degeneration effect is not a consequence ofnn-section itself. For everyn≥2n\geq 2, the largest-anglenn-sections produce partitions satisfying the minimum angle condition (and, therefore, the maximum angle condition). More precisely, if the initial triangle has its smallest angleγ0>0\gamma_{0}>0, then all descendant triangles have angles bounded below bymn=min⁡{γ0,π3​n},m_{n}=\min\left\{\gamma_{0},\frac{\pi}{3n}\right\},and, correspondingly, bounded above byπ−2​mn<π\pi-2m_{n}<\pi. We also show that the recursive largest-anglenn-section algorithm always produces a family of triangular partitions, i.e. the maximum diameter of level-kkdescendants tends to zero ask→∞k\to\infty.

## 1Introduction

Mesh refinement procedures are central in various adaptive finite element computations. A basic quality requirement is that the refinement process should not create arbitrarily degenerating mesh elements. In two dimensions, this is often expressed through the minimum angle condition: there should be a positive lower bound for all angles appearing in the refinement process. A weaker, but still important, requirement is the maximum angle condition, which requires that all maximum angles produced remain bounded away fromπ\pi.

The longest-edge bisection procedure is the classical example of a stable refinement rule. Rosenberg and Stenger proved that longest-edge bisection preserves a positive lower bound on angles in terms of the minimum angle of the initial triangle[1]. Longest-edge trisection is also known to be nondegenerate; Plaza, Suarez, Padron, and Falcon proved a positive minimum-angle bound for the longest-edge trisection[2]. The behavior changes for higher sections. In fact, Suarez, Moreno, Abad, and Plaza proved that longest-edgenn-sections produce degenerating triangles forn≥4n\geq 4, in the sense that one can generate triangles whose minimum angles tend to zero[3]. Later, Perdomo and Plaza presented a shorter proof of the same degeneracy phenomenon using a complex-variable normalization of triangle shapes[4]. Korotov, Plaza, and Suarez showed that the conforming longest-edgenn-section algorithm violates even the weaker maximum angle condition forn≥4n\geq 4[5].

These results suggest a natural question: is the degeneracy for largenncaused by the act of dividing into many parts, or by the fact that the divided object is the longest edge? The purpose of this paper is to show that the latter is the decisive feature. If, instead of dividing the longest edge, one divides the largest angle, then a simple regularity mechanism holds for everyn≥2n\geq 2.

The largest-angle bisection was recently studied by Ismailescu, Kim, Kim, and Lee, who proved, among other properties, that the procedure has the expected non-degeneracy behavior[6]. The present paper records the observation that the same regularity mechanism extends directly to largest-anglenn-section for everyn≥2n\geq 2. The key point is that the (largest) angle being divided is always at leastπ/3\pi/3. Hence each newly created angle is at leastπ/(3​n)\pi/(3n).

In Section2, we define the largest-anglenn-section directly in terms of angle triples. Section3contains the proofs for validity of the minimum/maximum angle conditions, and for the convergence of element diameters to zero. Section4gives a brief conclusion.

## 2Largest-anglenn-section rule

LetTTbe a nondegenerate triangle with anglesα,β,γ>0,α+β+γ=π.\alpha,\beta,\gamma>0,\qquad\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\pi.

A largest angle is any one of the angles equal tomax⁡{α,β,γ}.\max\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\}.

If there is more than one largest angle, one of them is chosen arbitrarily. This choice will not affect the estimates below.

Suppose, after relabelling the vertices ofTTif necessary, thatα=max⁡{α,β,γ}.\alpha=\max\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\}.

The largest-anglenn-section ofTTis obtained by dividing the angleα\alphaintonnequal parts and joining the corresponding division rays to the opposite side. This producesnnchild triangles. Reading off the angles of these children gives the following angle triples:Tj=(αn,β+j​αn,γ+(n−1−j)​αn),j=0,1,…,n−1.T_{j}=\left(\frac{\alpha}{n},\beta+\frac{j\alpha}{n},\gamma+\frac{(n-1-j)\alpha}{n}\right),\qquad j=0,1,\ldots,n-1.(1)

Indeed, thejjth child contains one sector angleα/n\alpha/n, receivesjjadjacent sectors on the side of the angleβ\beta, and receives the remainingn−1−jn-1-jadjacent sectors on the side of the angleγ\gamma. The sum of the three entries in (1) isαn+β+j​αn+γ+(n−1−j)​αn=α+β+γ=π,\frac{\alpha}{n}+\beta+\frac{j\alpha}{n}+\gamma+\frac{(n-1-j)\alpha}{n}=\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\pi,

so each triple is really the angle triple of a triangle, see figure1.Figure 1:The largest-anglenn-section of the triangleA​B​CABC, whose largest angleα\alphais divided intonnequal parts. The child triangleTjT_{j}, between the raysA​DjAD_{j}andA​Dj+1AD_{j+1}, has an angle triple(αn,β+j​αn,γ+(n−1−j)​αn).\left(\frac{\alpha}{n},\beta+\frac{j\alpha}{n},\gamma+\frac{(n-1-j)\alpha}{n}\right).

Starting from a single triangleT0T_{0}, recursive largest-anglenn-section means applying the above rule to every triangle in the current generation. We denote by𝒯k\mathcal{T}_{k}the set ofnkn^{k}triangles obtained afterkkgenerations. More generally, if one starts from a finite collection of initial triangles (initial triangulation), the same estimates apply to all descendants of all initial triangles. No conformity assertion for global triangular partitions is needed in this note; the estimates are purely element-wise.

## 3Regularity and diameter convergence properties

We now prove the main result, which contrasts sharply with the known behavior of the longest-edgenn-section forn≥4n\geq 4.

## Theorem 3.1(Regularity of the largest-anglenn-section).

Let𝒯k\mathcal{T}_{k}be the set of descendants (kk-th generation) obtained afterkksteps of recursive largest-anglenn-section. Definemn=min⁡{γ0,π3​n}.m_{n}=\min\left\{\gamma_{0},\frac{\pi}{3n}\right\}.(2)

Then every angle of every triangle in every generation produced satisfiesθ≥mn.\theta\geq m_{n}.(3)

Consequently, any ever produced angle satisfies also the following upper boundθ≤π−2​mn<π.\theta\leq\pi-2m_{n}<\pi.(4)

Thus, the largest-anglenn-section algorithm always produces sets of triangles satisfying both, the minimum angle condition and the maximum angle condition.

The initial triangle has all angles at leastγ0\gamma_{0}, and by definitionmn≤γ0m_{n}\leq\gamma_{0}. Thus the bound (3) follows by induction over the generations.

## Remark 3.2.

The lower bound (2) depends on the initial triangle and onnn. It is not uniform over all triangles in the initial triangulation as the initial anglesγ0\gamma_{0}can vary considerably. It is, however, uniform over the entire refinement tree generated from a fixed nondegenerate initial triangle.

We shall now prove that recursive largest-anglenn-section produces a (refining) family of triangular partitions, in the sense that the maximum diameter of the level-kkdescendants tends to zero. The proof uses an explicit area contraction estimate.

## Remark 3.6.

The argument does not require the longest edge of every child to be strictly shorter than the longest edge of its parent. Such a one-step statement can fail, for instance when a child inherits one side of the parent triangle. Instead, the proof uses an explicit uniform area contraction together with the minimum angle condition.

## 4Conclusion

The longest-edgenn-section and the largest-anglenn-section algorithms behave differently for large values ofnn. The known theory of the longest-edge mesh refinements shows that bisection and trisection produce nondegenerate triangular partitions, but the longest-edgenn-section, forn≥4n\geq 4, always produce sequences of degenerating triangles[1,2,3,4,5]. In contrast, the largest-anglenn-section remains regular for everyn≥2n\geq 2.

The reason for such a difference in the performance of the algorithms is essentially based on the following observation. The angle divided by the largest-anglenn-section is always at leastπ/3\pi/3. Therefore, each newly created sector angle is at leastπ/(3​n)\pi/(3n). This gives the uniform lower bound (and also the uniform upper bound) for every descendant angle in terms of the initial smallest angle andnn. Together with a compactness-based area contraction argument, this also implies that the recursive largest-anglenn-sections produce descendants whose all the diameters tend to zero.

Thus, the degeneration observed for the longest-edgenn-section whenn≥4n\geq 4is not an inevitable consequence of dividing a triangle into many subtriangles. It is tied to the longest-edge selection rule. The largest-angle selection rule avoids this particular instability and provides a regularnn-section refinement procedure for alln≥2n\geq 2.
